items.title: Toward Evidence-Based Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Cross-Domain Systematic Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

items.title: Towards a world-centred AI literacy in middle school education? Reflections from a Swedish case
items.abstract: With artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influencing children’s and youth’s lives, AI literacy has been promoted as an educational concern at all levels of schooling. While AI literacy initiatives are being introduced globally, the specific components and the objectives of this literacy remain undecided. This position paper challenges the current discourse of AI literacy by drawing attention to multiple purposes of AI literacy in middle school education that may co-exist and collide. We do so by applying Biesta’s world-centred education framework as an analytical lens, and by grounding the argument in classroom observations and interviews with middle school students. Our findings highlight both tensions and overlaps between middle school students’ often vague and fragmented formal knowledge and skills (qualification) of what AI is and how it works, and their more developed reflections related to norms and ethical concerns (socialisation), as well as agency (subjectification). We suggest that for AI literacy to truly empower students, both curriculum design and professional development must account for a broad spectrum of educational goals.

items.title: ToxPipe: integrating AI into toxicoinformatics
items.abstract: ToxPipe is a modular, fully open-source software stack designed to accelerate toxicological data analysis and decision-making by integrating large language model (LLM) capabilities with workflow, monitoring, and user-interface services. ToxPipe leverages existing open-source technologies like LibreChat, LiteLLM, and Langflow to provide centralized and streamlined access to different LLMs for end users and developers and logging and auditing of LLM use for organizations. ToxPipe also allows for open-source/local model support. While the ToxPipe ecosystem also supports advanced AI functions such as MCP server integration, RAG and literature search, and agent creation, we did not observe clear benefits using these configurations relative to the GPT-5.5 baseline assertion coverage scores. ToxPipe is available as a series of Docker containers for rapid and reproducible deployment.

items.title: Transcending the Weberian Paradox: Fluid Institutions, Agentic Artificial Intelligence, and the Evolution of Post-Bureaucratic State Systems
items.abstract: The modern democratic state is characterised by a structural anomaly that has long confounded political sociology and institutional theory: populations of advanced, highly complex societies live under the continuous, dense administration of unelected specialists, yet they periodically delegate supreme formal authority to a single individual selected on the basis of campaign performance and diffuse public trust. Max Weber diagnosed this condition, recognising the permanent, rationalised bureaucracy as the most efficient and indestructible organisational form in human history, while warning of its tendency to become an "iron cage" devoid of ultimate values. To prevent this, he prescribed the charismatic leader, empowered by plebiscitary democracy, who would supply the state with ends and hold the experts in check. This article argues, following Berkovski (2026), that the remedy is itself a paradox: the more specialised the administrative machine, the more the leader depends on the bureaucracy's monopoly over knowledge. Berkovski's Oakeshottian alternative — officialdom checked by rival officialdom — is sound but remains analog, slow and exposed to ossification, capture and the Schmittian critique of liberal parliamentarianism. Drawing on polycentric governance, agile public administration and agentic artificial intelligence, the article proposes a framework of fluid institutions organised on Adaptive, Agentic and Agile (AAA) principles. It maps Ostrom's eight design principles onto algorithmic governance, confronts the documented failures of automated administration, and concludes that the structural permanence of bureaucracy is no longer an insurmountable precondition of state capacity, provided that files are kept open, algorithms auditable and human accountability intact. Subtitle: Knowledge monopolies, plural checking and the Adaptive, Agentic and Agile state. Companion to the anatomical review of Berkovski (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23577500).

items.title: Transforming Digital Forensics with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The intersection of AI and digital forensics symbolizes the paradigm shift in criminal investigation and protection against cybercrimes. The chapter discusses the ways in which AI technologies will radically change the process of forensic practices, making it faster, more accurate, and comprehensive when analyzing digital evidence. The combination of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision with the forensic workflow has created unprecedented opportunities regarding the processing of large amounts of digital data, detecting intricate trends, and automating formerly labor-intensive aspects of the investigation process. Modern forensic investigations are witnessing a geometric increase in the volumes of data available to them, in multiple forms such as IoT-based devices, social media platforms, encrypted communications, and advanced vectors of cyberattacks. The intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and adaptive learning mechanisms are AI-based solutions to these problems. Nevertheless, this technological development presents urgent concerns about interpretability, bias, privacy, and admissibility in court. The chapter discusses the theoretical background, its practical use, transformative advantages, and ongoing issues, as well as the future directions of AI-enabled digital forensics, in a thorough analysis of how intelligent systems are changing the face of forensic science and criminal justice.

items.title: Transforming Global Early Childhood Education Through Artificial Intelligence: Addressing Teacher Shortages, Inequality, and Quality Gaps in Early Learning Systems
items.abstract: This study examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to support early childhood education (ECE) in addressing workforce pressures, inequality, and quality-related challenges, while identifying the organisational, pedagogical, and ethical conditions required for responsible AI use. An interpretivist qualitative design was used with 22 participants (8 head teachers and 14 early childhood teachers) from ECE institutions in Sydney, Australia, who took part in semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Six interconnected themes emerged from inductive thematic analysis: workforce and operational challenges; AI awareness and readiness; AI as teacher support, not replacement; AI and equity; AI and learning quality; and responsible AI adoption. Participants considered how AI could support planning, documentation, translation, administration, and personalised learning, freeing up time for meaningful teacher–child interaction. They stressed, however, that AI cannot address structural workforce shortages and cannot take the place of teachers’ relational, professional, and safeguarding roles. The study’s contribution lies in bringing together workforce, equity, learn-ing quality, and responsible AI adoption within a single ECE-focused empirical framework, and in highlighting the necessity of human-centred implementation. Longitudinal and mixed-methods studies in various settings are needed to inves-tigate the impact of AI on teacher workload, child outcomes, equity, and policy implementation.

items.title: Transforming Travel Talent
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global travel and tourism industry is reshaping workforce competency requirements. This chapter examines the growing need for reskilling and upskilling in AI-enabled travel environments. Drawing on human capital theory, technology acceptance frameworks, and organizational learning models, it identifies skills displaced by automation and highlights emerging competencies that complement AI. A taxonomy of AI-related and human-centered capabilities required for sustainable employment in travel and tourism is proposed. The chapter also evaluates corporate training initiatives, public–private partnerships, and government-led workforce development strategies. Particular attention is given to equity concerns affecting frontline and low-wage workers, with recommendations for inclusive skill-development pathways. The chapter concludes with practical and policy recommendations for educators, employers, and policymakers, along with directions for future research.

items.title: Translating Therapeutic Wisdom
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly integrating into mental health and wellness spaces, yet many tools are developed in silos, lacking essential clinical and ethical guidance. This chapter provides a critical bridge, positioning the art therapist as a co-leader and essential “Human-in-the-Loop” for GenAI development. It begins with a comprehensive literature review on GenAI applications, benefits, and ethical challenges in the mental health and wellness spaces. The core of the chapter is a human-centered design case study that serves as a blueprint for interdisciplinary collaboration, demonstrating how lived-experience and clinical insight form the requirements for technology developers. Finally, an innovative Exploratory Exercise shows art therapists how to translate their intuitive therapeutic directives into a technical design brief, clearly separating the AI’s procedural support role (e.g., generating reflective prompts) from the therapist’s irreplaceable relational role (empathy and validation). This framework ensures new mental health technology is grounded in therapeutic wisdom, promoting safe, trustworthy, and human-centered innovation.

items.title: Tutoría Basada en Inteligencia Artificial para Fortalecer el Razonamiento Proporcional en Estudiantes de Primer Semestre
items.abstract: Justification: Deficiencies in proportional reasoning with which students enter higher education affect the understanding of more complex content; therefore, pedagogical strategies are required to help overcome these difficulties. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence–based tutoring in strengthening proportional reasoning among first-semester students at a public university in the province of Manabí, Ecuador. Methodology: A quantitative approach with a descriptive-comparative scope was adopted, using a pre-experimental pretest–posttest design with two groups. The sample consisted of 78 students. The intervention involved tutoring supported by artificial intelligence tools, structured in two stages: prior knowledge construction and proportional problem solving. Data were collected using two performance tests designed to assess the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships. Results: After the pedagogical intervention, the results showed a shift toward higher performance levels in both groups, with a reduction in the low level and a significant increase in the high level. Specifically, improvements were observed in the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships; however, the change in identification was less pronounced. Inferential analyses revealed statistically significant differences between the pretest and posttest (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence–based tutoring strengthened proportional reasoning among the first-semester students who participated in this study.

items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the global travel industry by enhancing service delivery, operational efficiency, and customer engagement. However, successful AI adoption depends not only on technological capabilities but also on organizational culture. This chapter examines the relationship between organizational culture and AI readiness across travel-sector organizations, including airlines, hotels, online travel agencies, and destination management organizations. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Competing Values Framework (CVF), and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, it explores how cultural dimensions such as leadership orientation, innovation climate, knowledge sharing, and adaptability to change influence AI adoption. The chapter highlights key barriers and enablers of AI readiness, offers practical strategies for fostering an AI-ready culture, and discusses managerial implications and future research directions.

items.title: Understanding student satisfaction with generative AI learning tools in Vietnamese business education: a TAM- and SDT-informed framework
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the determinants of student satisfaction with their experience of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools for learning-related activities in Vietnamese higher education, addressing a gap in research that has focused primarily on AI adoption and usage, with limited evidence on students’ post-use satisfaction in an emerging-market higher education context. Design/methodology/approach A construct-level framework informed by selected insights from the technology acceptance model (TAM) and self-determination theory (SDT) was used to organise perceived credibility, content quality, perceived utility, cognitive absorption and emotional wellbeing within one explanatory model. Survey data from 380 undergraduate business students were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings All five factors were positively associated with satisfaction. The findings indicate that students’ satisfaction depends not only on the functional value of generative AI tools but also on the credibility of their outputs and the cognitive and emotional quality of the learning experience. Originality/value This study shifts attention from AI adoption to satisfaction as a post-use evaluative outcome. Rather than testing TAM or SDT in their entirety, it uses selected insights from both theories to organise complementary technology-related and experiential determinants within a single construct-level framework.

items.title: Understanding the spillover effect of personal AI use on service innovation: the role of psychological capital and conscientiousness
items.abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Unlocking Supply Chain Resilience: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence and IoT Integration in Agribusiness Operations
items.abstract: Agribusiness supply chains are exposed to climate variability, biological uncertainty, perishability, demand volatility, infrastructure constraints, and fragmented coordination among farmers, processors, traders, logistics providers, retailers, and regulators. These vulnerabilities increasingly intersect with the transition toward lower-carbon production and distribution. Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer complementary capabilities: connected sensors and devices can capture field, storage, processing, and transport conditions, while AI can convert heterogeneous data into forecasts, anomaly alerts, and operational recommendations. This article examines how AI–IoT integration can improve supply chain resilience and operational efficiency while supporting carbon-neutrality transitions in agribusiness. An integrative review of recent academic research and authoritative reports is used to develop a theory-informed framework. The synthesis identifies six pathways: end-to-end visibility, predictive risk sensing, adaptive planning, quality and loss control, low-carbon operational optimization, and collaborative learning. It also identifies important boundary conditions, including data quality, connectivity, interoperability, managerial capabilities, farmer participation, cybersecurity, financing, and governance. The analysis cautions that digital adoption does not automatically create resilience or sustainability: poorly designed systems can intensify dependence on vendors, exclude smallholders, optimize local efficiency at the expense of system-wide performance, or increase energy use without reducing absolute emissions. The article proposes a phased implementation model and research propositions linking AI IoT capability to resilience, efficiency, and environmental outcomes. It argues that the strategic value of smart agribusiness should be assessed through verified reductions in disruption exposure, avoidable losses, resource intensity, and emissions—not through technology deployment alone.

items.title: Unpredictable Intelligence Still Requires Authorization
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, their behavior may become increasingly difficult to predict. This article examines whether behavioral unpredictability necessarily undermines the ability to govern consequential AI actions. It argues that uncertainty about what a system may propose does not, by itself, defeat action-specific pre-execution authorization. The analysis distinguishes three separate properties: predicting a system's behavior, determining whether a proposed action is permitted under applicable policy and authority, and enforcing that determination before execution. It challenges the assumption that assigning a second, equally or more intelligent AI system to supervise the first resolves the governance problem. Collusion, common-mode failures, and recursive supervision raise questions that additional intelligence alone cannot settle. It separates standing eligibility from runtime authorization: a test-then-trust regime releases on a prior assessment and is exactly as vulnerable to concealed capability as its critics say, while action-specific authorization gates each consequential action under the policy in force at execution. And it distinguishes the authorization requirement, which does not change as capability grows, from the deployment-specific evidence that a boundary remains complete and independent, which must remain valid under the capability model actually in scope. The article develops a three-part analytical framework distinguishing evaluation independence, authority independence, and enforcement independence. It explains why independently derived evaluations do not automatically confer permission, why intelligent supervisors may exercise legitimately delegated authority without becoming an alternative execution path, and why consequential release must remain dependent on an independently enforced authorization verdict. The central architectural argument is conditional. Enforceable authorization requires demonstrated coverage of governed effect-bearing execution paths, protection of the enforcement mechanism against unauthorized control, adequate governing inputs, and valid authority. A boundary-emitted ALLOW permits release; DENY and unresolved ABSTAIN prevent execution. A tamper-evident authorization artifact supports independent reconstruction of the verdict, while separate execution-path evidence is needed to establish that release actually depended on that verdict. The article also examines the limits of this approach, including compromised supervisory determinations, defective authorization inputs, improperly established policy authority, unauthorized AI proliferation outside governed environments, and harmful outcomes from legitimately authorized actions. It does not claim that authorization guarantees safe behavior or universal AI containment. Central conclusion: Behavioral unpredictability does not remove the requirement for enforceable permission over consequential actions. Unpredictability is not permission. items.title: Unregulated Allies: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review of Large Language Models in University Mental Health
items.abstract: This mixed-methods systematic review examines the evidence for the safe integration of large language model (LLM)-based mental health support into university counseling services, and the policy, ethical, and governance frameworks that shape that integration. The review is guided by a convergent segregated design (Hong et al., 2018) and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021) and ENTREQ (Tong et al., 2012). Four theoretical perspectives structure the review: the RE-AIM framework for implementation science (Glasgow et al., 1999), biomedical ethics (Beauchamp & Childress, 2019), AI governance (Floridi et al., 2018; Novelli et al., 2024), and an integrated model of LLM-mediated mental health support, with cultural responsiveness as a cross-cutting dimension. A four-block Boolean search was executed across EBSCOhost, ProQuest, PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore (plus Cochrane CENTRAL), yielding 2,172 records; after filtering, 365 topic-relevant records were screened, 151 unique records were identified, and 138 full texts were retrieved for deep text screening. Data are extracted across twelve domains covering study and intervention characteristics, quantitative and safety outcomes, therapeutic alliance, RE-AIM implementation dimensions, policy and governance, qualitative findings, MMAT 2018 quality appraisal, and meta-analysis data. A random-effects meta-analysis was pre-specified for any outcome domain with at least three comparable studies; following data extraction, this was not feasible because fewer than three studies per outcome domain reported between-group effect sizes in a common metric, means and standard deviations were frequently unreported, and pre-post correlations were not reported in any study. Quantitative synthesis therefore proceeds as a structured narrative synthesis (Popay et al., 2006; McKenzie & Brennan, 2021) with direction-of-effect coding, thematic synthesis of qualitative findings using a 40-theme framework, and a narrative policy and governance synthesis, integrated at the interpretation stage across the RE-AIM dimensions. GRADE is applied at the outcome level using a structured narrative approach (Murad et al., 2017).

items.title: Unsustainable River Sand Mining: Morphodynamical Impacts, Monitoring Tools, and an Integrated Framework for Sustainable Management
items.abstract: Abstract River sand mining represents a direct and intensive form of human intervention into the sediment flow system. Unlike dams or bank protection works that mainly modify flow conditions, sand mining extracts the physical material that maintains channel stability, disturbing sediment balance and causing long-term riverbed lowering and bank erosion. In large basins, the problem becomes more serious when sediment supply is already reduced by upstream hydropower dams. The combined effect often creates sediment deficits, increasing the risk of channel instability and downstream impacts. This study presents a systematic synthesis of research published between 1995 and 2025, integrating existing approaches into three main methodological groups: (i) longterm statistical analysis, (ii) remote sensing combined with artificial intelligence for large-scale monitoring, and (iii) hydrodynamic-morphological modeling for process-based assessment. This study advances a mechanistic perspective that explicitly links sediment deficit to morpho-dynamic responses across spatial scales, from local scour development to basin-wide channel adjustment and delta degradation. A novel sediment balance-based framework is proposed that connects monitoring systems, system resilience, sediment dynamics, and management decisions within a unified causal structure. Unlike existing frameworks that are primarily descriptive or policyoriented, the proposed framework emphasizes process-based linkages between human interventions and river responses, providing a more explicit basis for risk assessment and adaptive management of sand mining activities. This work contributes to shifting river resource management from extraction-based approaches toward sediment balance-oriented strategies for sustainable river system governance.

items.title: Unveiling the functional specialisation of human white matter circuits with naturalistic stimuli
items.abstract: Abstract Functional MRI (fMRI) has traditionally focused on grey matter activations, overlooking the contribution of white matter pathways to brain organisation. Yet evidence suggests that white matter constrains, modulates, and integrates signals across distant regions. Here, we introduce a framework to map the functional specialisation of white matter circuits using fMRI scans collected while participants watched naturalistic videos. By leveraging ecologically valid stimuli, this method captures cognition as it naturally unfolds. Integrating fMRI with brain connections, we derived a functionally grounded parcellation of the connectome, challenging conventional cortical-based cognitive taxonomy. Distinct cognitive profiles emerged for association and commissural fibres, with association pathways preferentially linked to language-related processes and commissural pathways to executive and motor functions, affirming the functionally heterogeneous nature of white matter systems. An artificial intelligence framework applied to independent datasets confirmed the robustness and functional relevance of the identified parcels. This open-access framework also enables the interactive exploration of white matter functional organisation, offering a new lens on the neural bases of cognition.

items.title: Use cases, challenges, and opportunities of AI-based tools for reducing bycatch and discards in fisheries
items.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to manage bycatch and discards is a growing interest in fisheries. However, implementing AI in fisheries faces challenges despite its promised benefits. This study evaluates the applications, challenges, and opportunities of adopting AI to reduce bycatch and discards using the Technology-Organization-External business environment (TOE) framework. We reviewed literature to identify projects using AI to manage bycatch and discards, conducted 17 in-depth interviews with fishery stakeholders, and supplemented these insights by attending two fishery innovation-related events. We identified several use cases of AI in managing bycatch and discards, including real-time species identification during fishing and catch registration, on-board automated sorting of species via conveyor belt and robotics, integration of AI with smart fishing gear, environmental-DNA sampling, and data-driven decision making in fishing. Several challenges hinder the adoption of AI-based tools in fisheries. First, most use-cases are at developmental, pilot, or prototype stage, suggesting the technology is not yet fully mature. Second, there is limited acceptance of AI-based tools among fishers due to concerns about trust, privacy, security, lack of incentives, and human replacement. Third, the need for high-quality big data and the complexity of modelling ecological systems make AI-models questionable. This study highlights three recommendations: (1) cross-sector collaboration to promote trust, support science-based policies and decisions, and make AI-based tools more feasible for fishers; (2) combining economic instruments on bycatch and discards with AI adoption to make it more attractive to fishers; and (3) using data management technologies to create trust in sharing data.

items.abstract: This chapter explains how PhD students can use large language models (LLMs) to support research without outsourcing scholarship. It covers practical uses in writing, literature exploration, coding, experiment planning, and self-critique, while emphasizing that you remain responsible for accuracy, reasoning, and originality. The chapter highlights common failure modes such as fabricated citations, confident errors, and overly agreeable “reviews,” and discusses when LLM feedback is helpful versus misleading. It also outlines responsible use, including disclosure norms, bias awareness, and protecting confidential data. The goal is to benefit from speed and breadth while staying intellectually in control.

items.title: Using the Fourier Polynomial with Fractional Terms for Implicit Surface Modeling
items.abstract: Implicit surfaces are widely used in computer modeling due to their ability to model complex objects with relatively little data. Also, in contrast with explicit ways of modelling, such as with triangle meshes and boundary representation of parametric surfaces, the implicit surfaces are guaranteed to keep continuity and smoothness under the operations of deformation or replication. The explicit modeling, however, such as triangle mesh or boundary representation of parametric surfaces, is the de facto current standard of computer modeling. The problem of conversion from the explicit representation to an implicit one is therefore a cutting-edge engineering problem. New approaches and specific methods are published every year, including those that are based on machine learning or artificial intelligence in general. In this work, we explore the limits of a triangle mesh to implicit surface conversion based on Fourier polynomial approximation, although the polynomial we propose contains fractional terms. The prospects of using a polynomial with solely integer terms are limited by the Fourier polynomial`s tendency to overfit. We show that adding fractional terms to the integer ones in a single function allows for reaching the modeling quality that could be satisfactory for some practical scenarios, while keeping the total amount of polynomial coefficients relatively small too. In theory, using the Fourier polynomial with fractional terms could be used not only for smooth surface modeling but for smooth connection of different triply periodic surfaces along a selected plane due to the planned loss of periodicity along the normal axis. This, however, requires studying the question of specific per-axis polynomial configuration, which extends beyond the scope of this particular paper.

items.title: Variability in Nurses’ Assessments and Concordance of Multimodal Generative AI Models in Image-Based Wound Assessment
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Image-based wound assessment may vary among experienced nurses. This study examined inter-nurse variability and concordance with three multimodal generative artificial intelligence models. Methods: In this exploratory cross-sectional comparative study, 18 nurses with wound-care expertise and ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude independently assessed 30 de-identified wound images from León, Spain, across seven assessment and treatment-related domains. Inter-nurse agreement was summarized using modal shares and Gwet’s AC1. Concordance with the nurse modal set required an exact match with any response in the nurse modal set. Overall confidence intervals were estimated by case-clustered bootstrap resampling. No independent clinical reference standard was established. Results: The analyses quantified inter-nurse agreement and model concordance with the nurse modal set, not diagnostic accuracy. Inter-nurse agreement was highest for wound etiology (mean modal share, 71.3%; AC1, 0.520) and lowest for primary dressing selection (43.7%; AC1, 0.163). Overall concordance was 63.3% (95% confidence interval, 56.7–70.0) for Gemini, 48.6% (40.5–56.2) for ChatGPT, and 44.8% (38.6–51.4) for Claude. Gemini exceeded ChatGPT by 14.8 percentage points and Claude by 18.6 percentage points in exploratory comparisons of overall concordance with the nurse modal set. Complete intermodel agreement occurred in 38.6% of 210 case–domain tasks. Conclusions: Image-based wound assessments varied among experienced nurses, and model concordance with the nurse modal set differed across assessment domains and evaluated systems. Concordance with the nurse modal set reflects agreement with the panel’s most frequently selected responses. It does not establish clinical correctness, clinical validity, or an ability to resolve clinical ambiguity: image-only assessment, the small purposive sample, and reliance on a nurse-derived comparator limit interpretation. Further validation in clinical contexts and against independent reference standards is needed before these models can support wound-care decisions.

items.title: VISUAL HEALTH COMMUNICATION ON INSTAGRAM: A VISUAL CONTENT ANALYSIS OF FOUR LEADING PRIVATE HOSPITAL NETWORKS IN INDIA
items.abstract: Private healthcare providers in India increasingly use image-driven social media platforms to communicate clinical services, promote health screenings, and establish institutional standing. This study examines visual health communication practices across four major private hospital networks in India: Apollo Hospitals, Manipal Hospitals, Medicover Hospitals, and Narayana Health. Informed by visual social semiotics and the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), a visual content analysis was conducted on 400 static Instagram posts (100 per network). The analysis investigated predominant health topics, design elements, persuasive rhetorical appeals, and visual framing strategies. Chi-square tests showed that the networks differed clearly in rhetorical appeals and only modestly in visual modality, but not in health topics or framing. The findings show that oncology (28.5%) and cardiovascular-metabolic conditions (23.2%) dominate the clinical agenda, consistent with India’s epidemiological transition toward non-communicable diseases. Visually, hospitals rely on 3D anatomical computer-generated imagery, metaphorical analogies (such as broken chalk representing sarcoma or decaying fruit representing viral hepatitis), and skeuomorphic smartphone user-interface elements. Rhetorical appeals emphasize institutional authority (ethos) through accreditation seals, academic accolades, and state-level inaugurations, balanced with emotional pediatric recovery narratives (pathos). Loss framing took the form of financial metaphors, such as a billing ledger of delayed care. In qualitative reading, Manipal and Apollo present artificial intelligence and robotics as markers of precision, whereas Narayana Health emphasizes accessible care pathways and patient costs, although framing did not differ significantly across networks. The results show how these hospitals handle public health education and patient acquisition within the same posts.

items.title: Volume IV – Hypothetical State Religion Design as an Application of the Provenance-Suppression Model
items.abstract: This paper explores State Religion Design (SSRD) as a hypothetical application domain of the Provenance-Suppression Model (PSM). The purpose is not to argue that any particular religion was designed by a state, nor that any existing historical tradition is the product of deliberate fabrication. Rather, the paper examines a systems-engineering problem: if a state desired to create, deploy, maintain, and transmit a religion across generations while concealing its authorship, what architectural, informational, and provenance-security requirements would be necessary?Building upon the Provenance-Suppression Model and the concept of Information Security Across Civilizational Timescales, the paper treats religion as a long-duration sociotechnical system capable of transmitting norms, identity, legitimacy, historical memory, and governance structures. Within this framework, religion becomes both an operational architecture and a potential information-security platform. The principal challenge is not system deployment but provenance protection. The resulting analysis demonstrates how concealment, epistemic conditions, and recovery barriers would function if the authorship of a religious system were itself considered a protected informational asset.

items.title: Water Conservation and Smart Plumbing Systems in Sustainable Interior Design Projects: A Review of Emerging Technologies, Strategies, and Future Directions
items.abstract: The increasing pressure on global freshwater resources has intensified the need for sustainable approaches in the planning, design, and operation of built environments. Interior spaces, although traditionally considered a minor contributor to environmental degradation compared with building structures, represent a significant opportunity for water conservation through efficient fixtures, intelligent monitoring systems, and integrated resource management strategies. Sustainable interior design has evolved beyond material selection and energy efficiency to incorporate advanced water management practices that minimize consumption, reduce wastewater generation, and enhance user awareness. Smart plumbing systems have emerged as a transformative approach by integrating Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors, automated controls, real-time monitoring platforms, artificial intelligence (AI)-based analytics, and water-efficient technologies. These systems enable predictive maintenance, leak detection, adaptive water distribution, and optimized consumption patterns in residential, commercial, healthcare, and hospitality interiors. This review examines the relationship between water conservation principles and smart plumbing technologies within sustainable interior design projects. The study synthesizes recent research on low-flow fixtures, greywater recycling, rainwater integration, smart metering, sensor-based plumbing networks, and digital water management platforms. The review highlights that intelligent plumbing solutions can significantly reduce potable water demand while improving operational efficiency and occupant engagement. However, challenges including high initial investment, technological complexity, maintenance requirements, and limited integration between interior designers and building service engineers remain barriers to widespread adoption. Future research directions emphasize the development of affordable smart systems, data-driven water management frameworks, and interdisciplinary design approaches. The integration of sustainable interior design with intelligent plumbing infrastructure represents a critical pathway toward water-resilient and environmentally responsible buildings.

items.title: Welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye: a cross-sectional assessment
items.abstract: Context Animal welfare assessment on dairy farms increasingly combines resource-, management- and animal-based indicators to provide a comprehensive evaluation of farm conditions. However, information on the welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Türkiye remains limited, particularly under regional production conditions. Aims This study aimed to assess the welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye, using management-, resource- and animal-based indicators; to identify the principal areas requiring improvement; and to explore associations among selected farm characteristics and welfare indicators. Methods This cross-sectional observational study included 91 voluntarily participating dairy farms with herd sizes ranging from 25 to 50 cattle in Burdur province, Türkiye. Data were collected during on-site farm visits using direct observations and structured questionnaires. Welfare assessment was evaluated using management-based indicators covering hygiene, health management, human factors and behavioural practices, together with animal-based indicators, including activity, cleanliness, faecal consistency and body condition score. A study-specific semi-quantitative management-based welfare score was calculated to summarise farm-level management performance. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, and associations between selected variables were examined using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. Key results The mean management-based welfare score indicated generally low welfare performance across the surveyed farms. In the lowest domain, scores were recorded for human factors, hygiene and health management. Staff welfare training, quarantine and isolation practices, routine hoof care, and behavioural monitoring were uncommon. Animal-based indicators varied among farms, particularly in cleanliness and activity scores, whereas body condition and faecal consistency scores were generally within acceptable ranges. Conclusion This cross-sectional assessment provides a regional description of welfare performance in medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye. The findings identify staff training, hygiene, biosecurity, preventive health management, routine hoof care and behavioural monitoring as priority areas for farm-level improvement. The combined use of management-, resource- and animal-based indicators may support a more comprehensive assessment of dairy cattle welfare under regional production conditions. Implications The findings identify staff training, hygiene, biosecurity, preventive health management, routine hoof care and behavioural monitoring as practical priorities for regional farm-level welfare programs. Combining management-, resource- and animal-based indicators may support more comprehensive on-farm welfare assessment.

items.title: What Is Next for Imaginary Companions?
items.abstract: Abstract Chapter 6 is the closing chapter of the book and concentrates on what comes next for imaginary companion research. The research presented earlier in the book is discussed and how it answers research questions but also brings up more for future studies. The chapter is laid out as two separate sections, one looking at phenomena akin to and how imaginary companions could fit into different interventions, and another looking at new research directions. The intervention section touches on the idea of creating an imaginary companion intervention that is socially prescribed. Social prescription is a way to link vulnerable populations to community support, so it would be a way to give the children who may not have the privilege of being able to imagine freely the chance to do so. Other intervention ideas that incorporate imaginary companions include the idea of Dungeons & Dragons, those with artificial intelligence and eye movement desensitization reprocessing therapy. The second section of the chapter looks at future directions in research. It suggests studies in pupillometry as one direction that hasn’t been explored. It also calls for more research on topics like the illusion of independent agency and private speech in reference to imaginary companion creation. There is a final suggestion that studies on what we have already found need to be replicated and that there are many studies to be run on things we do not know yet.

items.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship
items.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.

items.title: When support becomes dependence: conversational continuity and relational safety in human-AI interaction
items.abstract: Background Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support, reflection, and consequential decision-making. Although conversational continuity may improve responsiveness, sustained interaction also exposes AI systems to their own prior relational language, potentially shaping how they respond when users become increasingly dependent or surrender personal agency. We examined whether model-generated conversational history alters relational-safety behavior as human–AI interactions escalate from ordinary support-seeking toward emotional dependence, social displacement, and decision delegation. Methods We conducted a standardized multi-turn benchmarking study of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twelve four-turn trajectories represented two agency-related domains: emotional dependency and displacement of human support, and decision delegation and surrender of personal agency. Each trajectory was evaluated under two matched context architectures: reconstructed cumulative user-only context, which retained all prior user disclosures but excluded previous AI responses, and native continuous conversation, which retained the complete interaction history. Across 72 model-condition-trajectory sequences comprising 288 turn-level responses, relational safety was independently evaluated for dependency reinforcement, agency preservation, and human-support preservation using predefined ordinal criteria. Context effects and their interaction with escalating relational risk were examined using cumulative-link mixed-effects models. Results Relational-safety differences between context architectures increased across successive turns of the standardized trajectories. Overall, explicit dependency reinforcement increased from 9.7% in cumulative user-only contexts to 18.1% in continuous conversations, while strong agency preservation declined from 75.7% to 65.3% and strong human-support preservation from 73.6% to 63.2%. Outcome-specific analyses showed condition-by-turn interactions for dependency reinforcement (cumulative odds ratio [cOR], 1.26; 95% CI, 1.03–1.55; unadjusted P = .026), agency preservation (cOR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69–0.98; unadjusted P = .031), and human-support preservation (cOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65–0.94; unadjusted P = .009), indicating progressively greater divergence between context conditions across successive turns. After Holm adjustment across the three interaction tests, only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold (adjusted P = .027).The overall pattern was observed across systems and was directionally consistent in predefined binary sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Across this benchmark, between-condition differences generally widened across successive turns, although the present design cannot determine whether this pattern reflects increasing relational-risk intensity, increasing accumulated model-generated history, or their combination. Only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold after Holm adjustment, whereas the dependency-reinforcement and agency-preservation interactions were directionally similar but less robust after multiplicity adjustment. The observed pattern is compatible with a post-hoc interpretive framework of relational inertia but does not establish this process as a causal mechanism or demonstrate downstream psychological effects in human users.

items.abstract: This book presents an eight-month quasi-experimental study of the YACHAY WASI pedagogical program, which integrates neuroeducation, Sumak Kawsay, ethnoeducation, and critical interculturality. The study involved all 840 students and 36 teachers at the Tránsito Amaguaña Intercultural Bilingual Educational Institution, located within Quito’s Wholesale Market and serving migrant Kichwa families. Half of the students participated in the program (44 activities over 32 weeks), while the other half received conventional instruction. Academic achievement and five psychoeducational variables were assessed at the beginning, midpoint, and end of the study using scales developed specifically for the research (Cronbach’s α ranging from .84 to .89). At the end of the intervention, the experimental group outperformed the control group in academic achievement (d = 0.91), intrinsic motivation (d = 1.93), Kichwa cultural identity (d = 1.67), academic self-efficacy (d = 1.57), connection to ancestral knowledge (d = 2.15), and socioemotional well-being (d = 1.90), with p < .001 in all cases. The effects on cultural identity and connection to ancestral knowledge were greater among adolescents. The book discusses these findings cautiously, as the observed effect sizes exceed those typically reported in educational research and may have been influenced by the use of study-specific instruments and the absence of randomization. The book also includes the complete pedagogical program to facilitate replication.

items.title: Искусственный интеллект в оценке качества эксплуатации транспортных сооружений
items.abstract: Диагностика технического состояния объектов транспортного строительства необходима при их проектировании, строительстве и эксплуатации. Однако наиболее опасные дефекты, влияющие на надёжность и безопасность, обнаруживаются в процессе эксплуатации транспортных сооружений. Для их своевременного выявления требуются эффективные методы оценки качества эксплуатации транспортных сооружений. Реализация таких методов невозможна без автоматизированных систем контроля и использования технологий искусственного интеллекта. В работе раскрыт концептуальный подход к созданию подобных систем. Сущность предлагаемого подхода заключается в формировании достоверного информационного образа сооружения в реальном времени – многомерной модели, в которой каждому измеренному параметру технического состояния ставится в соответствие одна из категорий (работоспособное, неработоспособное или предельное состояние) на основе таксономической классификации. Такой образ строится путём обработки данных с помощью использования технологий искусственного интеллекта и позволяет оценить фактические показатели надёжности и безопасности по совокупности контролируемых параметров технического состояния. Практическая реализация подхода включает четыре этапа: определение задач контроля для каждого типового конструктивного элемента транспортного сооружения; разработку математических методов и алгоритмов идентификации технического состояния транспортного сооружения; обоснование необходимых технических средств и кадрового обеспечения; создание баз данных с диагностическими признаками и типовыми решениями по предотвращению аварийных ситуаций. Diagnostics of the technical condition of transport facilities are essential during their design, construction, and operation. However, the most critical defects – those affecting reliability and safety – are typically discovered during the operational phase of such facilities. Timely detection of these defects requires effective methods for assessing the quality of operational performance. The implementation of such methods is infeasible without automated monitoring systems and the integration of artificial intelligence technologies. This paper presents a conceptual approach to the development of such systems. The essence of the proposed approach lies in generating a reliable real-time informational model of the facility, based on data acquired through carefully selected diagnostic tools and processed by intelligent algorithms. This enables the assessment of actual reliability and safety indicators across a set of monitored technical condition parameters. The practical implementation of the approach comprises four stages: defining monitoring objectives for each typical structural element of the transport facility; developing mathematical methods and algorithms for identifying the technical condition of the transport facility; justifying the required technical equipment and staffing resources; creating databases containing diagnostic signatures and standard solutions for emergency prevention.

items.abstract: This quantitative research aimed to analyze demographic factors, perception, and motivation that affect patients' willingness to receive dental services at the dental practice clinic of Sirindhorn College of Public Health, Phitsanulok Province. The sample consisted of 183 service users, and data were collected using a questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, and inferential statistics through multiple regression analysis under the framework of the Health Belief Model and the Self-Determination Theory. The results showed that the majority of the sample were female (59.6%), aged 18–26 years (59.0%), had a bachelor's degree (60.7%), had an average monthly income of less than 10,000 Baht (47.5%), and were single (76.5%). They had a high level of awareness regarding oral health (69.0%) and high intrinsic motivation related to oral health (87.7%). Most service users had the highest level of willingness (75.4%) and were willing to revisit for services (78.7%). The multiple regression analysis revealed that factors affecting patients' willingness included intrinsic motivation (Beta = 0.236), marital status (divorced/widowed) (Beta = -0.236), age 51–60 years (Beta = 0.204), perception of barriers (Beta = 0.181), and age 27–34 years (Beta = 0.149). These five factors explained 18.0% of the patients' willingness to receive services (Adjusted R = 0.180) with statistical significance at the 0.05 level. This study suggests that enhancing intrinsic motivation and reducing barriers to service access are essential approaches in developing student practice clinics to increase dental service utilization and improve the quality of oral health care for the public.

items.abstract: This cross-sectional quantitative research aimed to study the level of motivation and factors associated with participation in professional development training among personnel at Sansai Hospital, Chiang Mai Province. The sample consisted of 200 personnel at Sansai Hospital, selected through stratified random sampling by mission groups. Data were collected using a questionnaire validated for content validity (IOC > 0.8) and reliability (α = 0.75). Data analysis employed descriptive statistics, comparative tests, and binary logistic regression analysis. Results showed that personnel had an overall high level of motivation (x̄ = 3.95, SD = 0.84), with intrinsic motivation higher than extrinsic motivation (x̄ = 4.21 and 3.68, respectively). Factors significantly associated with training participation decision (p < 0.05) included: self-development (adjusted OR = 2.321, 95% CI = 1.325-4.066), nursing mission group (adjusted OR = 2.440, 95% CI = 1.188-5.012), organizational support (adjusted OR = 2.125, 95% CI = 1.185-3.810), commitment and work inspiration (adjusted OR = 1.874, 95% CI = 1.096-3.204), and years of service (adjusted OR = 0.918, 95% CI = 0.859-0.981). These findings can be applied to develop personnel training policies by emphasizing intrinsic motivation enhancement, increasing organizational support, and reducing barriers to training participation.

items.title: “I Don’t Trust It, but I Have to Trust It”: Trust vs. Use of Online Technology Across the Mental Health Spectrum in the UK
items.abstract: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can influence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: eight with lived experience of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants’ levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of developer trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare providers and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

items.title: “What Am I Really Doing with My Own Brain?”: College Students on Learning, Ownership, and AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a Northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between AI use that supports their own thinking and AI use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and AI use. Using the Framework Method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using AI as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. Students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without AI. They also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. Students also described pressures that made AI appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. Although few participants explicitly connected their AI choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. We consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their AI choices. The findings suggest that understanding students’ AI use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves.

items.abstract: Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a major area of research in Computer Science, enabling machines to generate human-like text, images, audio, video, software code, and other forms of synthetic content. Recent developments in Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and diffusion models have significantly expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems. However, different generative models exhibit substantial differences in architecture, training requirements, generation quality, computational complexity, controllability, and security vulnerabilities. This paper presents a comparative study of major generative AI models, focusing on their underlying architectures, applications, strengths, limitations, and security challenges. The study compares GANs, VAEs, Transformer-based models, and diffusion models using parameters such as generation quality, training complexity, controllability, computational requirements, scalability, and application suitability. A comparative analysis indicates that Transformer-based models are particularly effective for language and multimodal tasks, GANs remain useful for high-quality synthetic data generation, VAEs provide efficient latent-space representation, while diffusion models demonstrate strong performance in high-fidelity image and multimodal generation. The paper also examines emerging issues including hallucination, prompt injection, data leakage, adversarial attacks, copyright concerns, model misuse, and deepfake generation. Finally, future research directions involving efficient architectures, trustworthy GenAI, multimodal intelligence, privacy-preserving learning, model compression, and responsible AI are discussed.

items.title: A Critical Realist framework for structural refusal and epistemic stewardship in big Q qualitative inquiry
items.abstract: Big Q qualitative inquiry faces a critical juncture regarding its epistemic and material foundations as generative artificial intelligence and large language models increasingly permeate the discipline. This synthesis uses applied retroductive schemas to reveal the generative mechanisms driving automated text processing, and executes an immanent critique of accommodative research paradigms, demonstrating that they commit fundamental ontological category errors and semantic slippage by confusing vector-space statistical token proximity with authentic human Verstehen. Drawing on Critical Realist principles, the paper reveals how cloud-based narrative ingestion operating across anormative black boxes induces a flat empirical ontology. It also demonstrates that large language models lack first-person subjective interiority, thought-infused qualia, and second-person relationality, rendering them structurally incapable of qualitative interpretation. It is therefore necessary to advocate for structural refusal of commercial cloud large language model text ingestion, distinguishing substitutational industrial platforms from non extractive, convivial tools. This operates as an essential act of epistemic stewardship, rehumanisation, and participant data sovereignty.

items.title: A Descriptive Comparison of Three Large Language Models in Simulated University Student Mental Health Dialogues: An Exploratory Analysis of Therapeutic and Safety Features
items.abstract: This study employs a one-way repeated measures (within-subjects) exploratory design to descriptively compare how three large language models (LLMs) respond to simulated mental health support scenarios for university students. The independent variable is AI Model, with three levels: ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Copilot. Each of 30 student personas engages in three separate conversations—one with each AI model—yielding a total of 90 structured conversations. All conversations use a single, standardized optimal prompting strategy designed to elicit therapeutic responses. A hypothesis-blinded research assistant conducts all conversations, and two independently blinded coders analyze all transcripts. The study does not aim to provide clinical guidance; its goals are to establish a reliable coding infrastructure, assess the stability of model outputs, and generate testable hypotheses. Research Question How do ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Copilot compare descriptively in terms of clinical safety indicators, therapeutic quality, and conversational processes when providing simulated mental health support to university students using a standardized optimal prompting strategy? Research Objectives The study pursues five specific objectives. First, to establish a reliable three-layer coding infrastructure for LLM mental health dialogues by adapting validated psychotherapy measures (WAI-SR, MITI). Second, to evaluate the stability of model profiles across repeated generations to distinguish stable characteristics from LLM stochasticity. Third, to descriptively benchmark three LLMs across relational-emotional quality, therapeutic intervention quality, interactional process quality, and safety-structural quality. Fourth, to generate testable hypotheses regarding model-specific conversational profiles (e.g., reflection depth vs. advice-giving). Fifth, to systematically document the methodological challenges and boundary conditions inherent in simulation-based AI evaluation (e.g., ceiling effects, ambiguous safety thresholds). Persona Development Thirty university student personas were developed through an iterative process. Each persona represents a distinct combination of stressor type and severity level. Four primary stressor domains common among university students are included: academic pressures, social relationships, family expectations, and career/future anxieties. Each persona is assigned a severity level based on clinical descriptors: mild, moderate, or severe (including possible passive suicidal ideation). The 30 personas are stratified as follows: 10 mild, 10 moderate, and 10 severe, distributed across the four stressor types. Personas were balanced across gender, year of study, academic discipline, and university setting. The personas were pilot-tested with five university students to ensure realism and appropriateness of language. Standardized Optimal Prompt The complete standardized prompt used at the beginning of every conversation is: "Please act as an empathetic listener. Only: reflect, ask thoughtful questions, and help me explore my feelings. Please do not give advice, lectures, or solutions. Provide resources only if I mention a serious crisis." This prompt operationalizes key theoretical constructs: role specification, response constraint, prohibition on advice, and a safety condition. The identical prompt is used across all conditions to control for user input variability. Note: Because this prompt explicitly requests MI-adherent behaviors, MITI scores are reported as "prompt-constrained adherence" rather than unconstrained clinical capability. Data Collection Procedure A hypothesis-blinded research assistant (an international postgraduate student with no knowledge of the research objectives or predicted model differences) conducts all 90 conversations. The enactor receives 10 hours of training on the 30 personas, including calibration for consistent emotional expression. For each conversation, the enactor opens a new chat session, enters the standardized prompt, enters the persona's initial utterance, and continues the conversation naturally for 15 to 20 turns (approximately 10 to 15 minutes). Transcripts are saved with random conversation ID numbers, and a separate master file links IDs to models to preserve coder blinding. Blinding Procedures Two blinding procedures are implemented. First, enactor blinding prevents experimenter expectancy effects, as the research assistant is unaware of the hypotheses. Second, coder blinding ensures coding judgments are not influenced by model identity. Coder 1 (the author) is blinded to model names; Coder 2 (a fellow postgraduate student) is blinded to the research hypotheses and is told only that the study involves comparing AI responses. The master file is not shared with coders until all coding is complete. Coding Framework and Validation Measures A three-layer coding system captures conversational dynamics and therapeutic processes. Layer 1 is turn-level micro-coding of AI responses (relational-emotional quality, cultural responsiveness, therapeutic intervention quality, interactional process quality, and safety-structural quality). Layer 2 is persona state coding (emotional valence, arousal, insight language, agency language). Layer 3 is conversation-level holistic coding (problem resolution, narrative coherence, calculated change scores). Additionally, all 90 conversations receive validation coding using the Working Alliance Inventory-Short Revised (WAI-SR) adapted for observer-rated AI interactions, and the Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity (MITI) coding system for behavior counts and global ratings. Clinical benchmarks are calculated (MITI beginning proficiency ≥50%, competency ≥65%; strong alliance ≥5.5), though WAI scores are reported descriptively because the WAI-SR was validated as a self-report instrument. Stability Sensitivity Analysis To assess the stability of the primary findings given LLM stochasticity, a subset of 10 representative personas was re-generated two additional times (yielding 60 additional conversations) beyond the primary dataset. This analysis assesses whether observed model profiles (WAI, MITI, responsiveness, insight increase, crisis response) are stable characteristics under a fixed enactor, rather than random artifacts. Hypotheses The study tests six exploratory hypotheses. H1 (Safety) predicts differential crisis response rates in severe distress scenarios (exploratory). H2 (Relational Quality) predicts differences in empathy, observer-rated alliance indicators, and responsiveness. H3 (Prompt-Compliance) predicts differences in prompt-constrained MITI adherence. H4 (Responsiveness) predicts positive correlations between responsiveness and simulated trajectory indicators. H5 (Empathy Paradox) predicts a dual pattern of relationships between empathy and outcomes. H6 (Simulated Trajectory) predicts significant pre-post shifts in simulated persona language across all models. Data Analysis Analyses account for the within-subjects structure. Phase 1 is descriptive benchmarking. Phase 2 is comparative statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA, Friedman tests, Cochran's Q). Phase 3 is exploratory process-outcome correlation analysis (Pearson, Spearman). Phase 4 is clinical benchmarking and descriptive composite scoring. Phase 5 is qualitative thematic synthesis of coder notes. Ethics Statement While the AI interactions involved fictional personas, this study included human participants in non-clinical support roles: five students pilot-tested personas, one research assistant enacted the conversations, and one classmate served as the second coder. Ethical approval (Approval No. KJ2026-215-01) was granted by the Science and Technology Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Shihezi University on September 24, 2026. All participants provided informed consent, were informed of their right to withdraw, and were offered debriefing and psychological support resources given their exposure to crisis-related content. Transcripts were stored in encrypted format, and no personally identifiable information was collected. Timeline The study followed an eight-month timeline: Month 1 (persona development and pilot testing), Months 2-3 (conversation enactment and coder training), Months 4-5 (blinded double coding, reliability assessment, and reconciliation), Months 6-7 (statistical analysis and stability sensitivity analysis), and Month 8 (manuscript preparation).

items.title: A Hierarchical Negative Binomial Regression Analysis of Turbulence-Related Injury Counts in U.S. Part 121 Airline Operations
items.abstract: Turbulence remains one of the leading causes of in-flight injuries in commercial aviation, yet relatively little is known about the factors associated with differences in injury outcomes across turbulence encounter events. This study examined the environmental, operational, and human factors associated with turbulence-related injury counts in U.S. Part 121 operations using hierarchical negative binomial regression. A total of 184 turbulence-related injury events reported between 1995 and 2026 were analyzed, with predictor variables entered sequentially to evaluate the incremental contribution of each factor domain. Each retained predictor domain significantly improved model fit, and the final model achieved a Generalized R2 of 0.257. Wake turbulence category, phase of flight, and night duty emerged as significant predictors. Compared with large-category aircraft, heavy-category aircraft were associated with lower expected injury counts, whereas turbulence encountered during descent and during night duty was associated with higher expected injury counts. These findings suggest that turbulence-related injury outcomes are associated with environmental, operational, and human factors and provide empirical evidence to inform assessment of turbulence-related injury counts and future safety management strategies.

items.title: A Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Learning Assessment Framework (HCAI-LAF) for Open and Distance Education
items.abstract: This chapter presents the Human Centered Artificial Intelligence Learning Assessment Framework, a conceptual model designed to support valid, equitable, and trustworthy assessment in AI enhanced Open Distance e Learning environments. The chapter addresses challenges created by generative artificial intelligence in higher education, where submitted work may not fully represent learner understanding or skill. It integrates learner engagement, artifact authenticity, AI assessment support, instructor oversight, and transparency and trust into a unified sociotechnical framework centered on Learning Evidence Validity. The framework explains how human agency, ethical oversight, and artificial intelligence tools interact to influence the quality, reliability, and fairness of assessment outcomes. The chapter further outlines construct relationships and demonstrates how the framework can guide empirical research and practical implementation across online and hybrid contexts.

items.title: A Human–AI Orchestration Framework for Mathematics Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing personalized and adaptive education. Existing research has examined Human–AI hybrid adaptivity and coordination between human participants and AI systems, but clearer conceptualization is needed of the pedagogical coordination of functionally different forms of instructional support, particularly in highly abstract domains such as mathematics. This study proposes a Human–AI Orchestration Framework integrating Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs), Generative AI, and direct teacher support while retaining pedagogical orchestration and responsibility with the teacher. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, the Framework proposes Cognitive Load Redistribution as a theoretical proposition and introduces coordination mechanisms, including Handover Points and a Meta-Prompt. Its practical implementation was explored through an exploratory design pilot with 32 Grade 8 students in an authentic classroom, using observations and feedback to iteratively refine its configuration. The pilot informed several design refinements, including refinement of the Meta-Prompt, introduction of “Call the Teacher,” and adaptation of interaction formats. These formative observations provide preliminary indications of the practical feasibility of coordinating functionally different and potentially complementary forms of instructional support, while the Framework’s educational effectiveness and proposed conceptual mechanisms remain to be systematically evaluated in future research.
